objects.name: Opportunity Rover
objects.description: Opportunity landed on 25 January 2004 for a 90-sol mission and operated for nearly 15 years — over 55 times its planned lifetime. It drove 45.16 km across the Martian surface, the longest distance travelled by any off-Earth wheeled vehicle. A planet-wide dust storm in June 2018 blocked sunlight to its solar panels. Last contact: 10 June 2018.

objects.name: Eagle Crater
objects.description: Opportunity landed inside Eagle Crater, a small 22-metre impact crater. Scientists called it a 'hole in one'. The crater walls exposed layered bedrock containing tiny haematite spherules nicknamed 'blueberries'. This was the first in-situ evidence that liquid water once existed on the Martian surface.

objects.name: Haematite 'Blueberries'
objects.description: Scattered across Meridiani Planum, these small spherical concretions of grey haematite are typically 4–6 mm across. They formed inside water-saturated sedimentary rock and eroded out as the rock weathered. Their discovery was a landmark finding: definitive proof that Mars once had sustained liquid water on its surface.

objects.name: Heat Shield
objects.description: Opportunity drove to examine its own heat shield, which had impacted the surface about 250 metres from the landing site. Near the heat shield, the rover found an iron-nickel meteorite, later named Heat Shield Rock — the first meteorite identified on another planet. It confirmed that the Martian atmosphere was once thicker.

objects.name: Marathon Valley
objects.description: In March 2015, Opportunity reached Marathon Valley on the rim of Endeavour Crater, having driven 42.195 km — a full marathon distance. The valley contained clay minerals detected from orbit by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Clay minerals form in near-neutral water, suggesting this area once had conditions more hospitable to life.

objects.name: Perseverance Valley
objects.description: Opportunity's final resting place is in Perseverance Valley, a shallow channel carved into the western rim of Endeavour Crater. The rover was studying how the valley formed — by water, wind, or ice — when the 2018 global dust storm ended its mission. The valley was named for the rover's remarkable longevity.
